narrative:
Your application was denied because a predictive model determined that your chance of passing the bar exam on the first attempt is very low—only about 3%. In other words, the model estimated a 97% likelihood that you would fail, and that level of risk is not acceptable for admission.

The most important factors driving this decision were your academic standing in your third year, your LSAT score, and your academic standing in your first year, in that order of influence. All three pushed strongly toward a prediction of failure.

Your third-year class standing placed you in the bottom decile of your school, while students who were typically admitted fell near the middle of the distribution. This suggests that, even after several years of legal education, your performance remained far below the level needed to succeed on a high-stakes exam. Similarly, your first-year standing was also the very lowest decile, reinforcing the pattern of academic struggle from the start.

Your LSAT score of 23.50 is substantially below the average of about 37 among admitted students. Since the LSAT is designed to measure reasoning and reading comprehension skills essential for the bar exam, a score this low independently flagged serious risk.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking the LSAT after focused preparation, and look for ways to strengthen your academic record—such as repeating challenging courses or enrolling in a post-baccalaureate legal studies program. Demonstrating a sustained upward trend in performance would help counter the concerns raised by your earlier grades.
